results.question: What were TCS's two stated FY26 AI-related priorities: one focused on changing internal delivery and one focused on clients?
results.reference_answer: TCS aimed to embed AI in internal delivery to improve productivity, testing, operations and support, while selling AI-led transformation services to help clients redesign processes, build data foundations and deploy AI at scale.
results.answer: Internal delivery priority: AI coding assistants, automated testing and AI-supported operations to raise productivity. Client priority: data foundations, model deployment, agent-based automation and AI-enabled process redesign for clients.

passages.text: Repositioning for a changing services market Through FY26 TCS framed its strategy around artificial intelligence, both as something it sells and as a way of changing how it delivers work. Management stated that the company had moved from building capabilities to executing on revenue, citing annualised AI revenue above $2.3 billion in Q4.

From capability to revenue AI was the central theme of TCS's FY26 messaging. By Q4, the company reported annualised AI-related revenue above $2.3 billion, equal to more than 6% of total revenue. Where AI shows up in the business • Client engagements. Data foundations, model deployment, agent-based automation and AI-enabled process redesign for clients. • Internal delivery. AI coding assistants, automated testing and AI-supported operations to raise productivity. • People. More than 270,000 employees have higher proficiency in AI and machine learning. • Deal wins. Several of the mega deals signed during the year were described as including AI-led transformation components. Questions to watch • How much AI revenue is new versus relabelled existing work. • Whether productivity gains are passed on to clients through lower prices. • Whether AI revenue growth can offset slower growth in traditional application services. The definition of AI revenue is TCS's own. Figures are annualised run-rate, not full-year recognised revenue.

What TCS sells to its clients TCS organises its offerings around the full lifecycle of enterprise technology change. In broad terms the portfolio covers the following areas. • Consulting and strategy. Business and technology advisory to help clients plan large transformations. • Cloud and infrastructure. Migration, modernisation and managed operations across public, private and hybrid clouds. • Enterprise applications. Implementation and support of core platforms in finance, supply chain, human resources and customer management. • Data and artificial intelligence. Data engineering, analytics, machine learning and, increasingly, generative and agentic AI solutions. • Cybersecurity. Security strategy, monitoring, identity and response services. • Engineering and industrial technology. Product engineering, embedded systems, IoT and digital twins for manufacturing and other industries. • Business process services. Operations that combine automation with human expertise, such as finance and procurement operations. • Products and platforms. Industry platforms, notably in banking and financial services, education and retail. Clients typically engage TCS through multi-year programmes. Large deals are tracked as total contract value (TCV), which TCS reports each quarter.

Conditions shaping FY26 The global environment for technology services remained uncertain through FY26. In July 2025, TCS's CEO said continued macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty had caused a demand contraction. Clients delayed or scaled back discretionary projects while continuing to commit to cost-saving and modernisation work.

Restructuring in FY26 In 2025 TCS announced plans to reduce its workforce by about 12,000 employees, roughly 2% of the total, as part of a programme to realign skills with AI-led delivery and changing client demand. The headcount decline in Q2 and Q3 FY26 reflects this programme.

Investing in skills The scale of training is central to the TCS model: with more than half a million employees, even small changes in skills mix have large effects on productivity and revenue per person. Learning hours rose 23% in a year when headcount fell, so hours per employee rose sharply. Focus areas • Foundational and advanced AI skills, including generative and agentic AI. • Cloud, data and cybersecurity certifications. • Domain knowledge in banking, retail, manufacturing and life sciences. • Leadership development for mid-level managers.

• $40.7 billion of FY26 TCV provides revenue visibility. • Margins at a four-year high with room for further productivity gains. • AI revenue above a $2.3 billion annualised run rate. • Broader client base, with 66 clients above $100 million.

• Embed AI in delivery. Using AI tools to improve developer productivity, testing, operations and support. • Sell AI-led transformation. Helping clients redesign processes, build data foundations and deploy AI at scale. • Reskill the workforce. More than 270,000 employees have higher proficiency in AI and machine learning, and the company logged 69 million learning hours in the year. • Invest in infrastructure and partnerships. Building AI-ready capacity and alliances with technology providers. • Protect margins while investing. Delivering a 25% operating margin while funding new capabilities. The strategic trade-off is clear: AI can reduce the effort needed for traditional work, which pressures revenue per project, while opening new categories of demand. FY26 results suggest margin benefits are arriving earlier than top-line benefits.

results.question: What were TCS's FY26 operating margin and net margin?
results.reference_answer: FY26 operating margin was 25% and net margin was 19.8%.
results.answer: TCS's FY26 operating margin was 25% and net margin was 19.8%.

passages.text: Operating and net margin trends TCS reported an operating margin of 25% for FY26, up 70 basis points year on year and the highest in four years. In Q3, the operating margin was 25.2%. The net margin excluding exceptional items was 19.8%, up 80 basis points. Why margins improved • Lower cost of revenue. Cost of revenue fell from 60.9% of revenue in Q1 to 59.3% in Q4. • Productivity and automation. AI-assisted delivery reduced effort on parts of the work. • Workforce actions. Headcount was reduced through the middle of the year, lowering employee costs relative to revenue. • Currency. A weaker rupee raised the rupee value of dollar billings against largely rupee-denominated delivery costs. What could erode them • Wage increases and higher attrition. • Investment in AI infrastructure and training. • Pricing concessions on large renewals and vendor consolidation deals. • A reversal in the rupee.

A year of margin gains, record deal wins and workforce reset FY26 was a year of contrasts for TCS. Top-line growth in US dollar terms was flat to slightly negative, reflecting cautious discretionary technology spending among clients, particularly in banking and financial services and in North America. In rupee terms revenue still grew 4.6% to ₹267,021 crore, helped by currency. Profitability improved even as growth stayed muted. The operating margin reached 25%, the highest in four years, and the net margin excluding exceptional items rose to 19.8%. Management cited productivity from automation and AI-led delivery, tighter cost control and a more favourable mix.

What to follow in FY27 TCS ended FY26 with record deal momentum, a 25% operating margin and a workforce that had stopped shrinking. The main questions for FY27 concern how quickly that momentum turns into revenue growth.

Restructuring in FY26 In 2025 TCS announced plans to reduce its workforce by about 12,000 employees, roughly 2% of the total, as part of a programme to realign skills with AI-led delivery and changing client demand. The headcount decline in Q2 and Q3 FY26 reflects this programme.

• Embed AI in delivery. Using AI tools to improve developer productivity, testing, operations and support. • Sell AI-led transformation. Helping clients redesign processes, build data foundations and deploy AI at scale. • Reskill the workforce. More than 270,000 employees have higher proficiency in AI and machine learning, and the company logged 69 million learning hours in the year. • Invest in infrastructure and partnerships. Building AI-ready capacity and alliances with technology providers. • Protect margins while investing. Delivering a 25% operating margin while funding new capabilities. The strategic trade-off is clear: AI can reduce the effort needed for traditional work, which pressures revenue per project, while opening new categories of demand. FY26 results suggest margin benefits are arriving earlier than top-line benefits.

What to follow in FY27 TCS ended FY26 with record deal momentum, a 25% operating margin and a workforce that had stopped shrinking. The main questions for FY27 concern how quickly that momentum turns into revenue growth.

Cash conversion remained strong TCS generated cash flow from operations equal to 111.0% of net profit in FY26. Quarterly conversion was strong in each period. Conversion above 100% indicates that cash collections and working-capital management outpaced accounting profit. The Q3 figure of 130.4% reflects the effect of non-cash exceptional charges in that quarter, which reduced reported profit but not cash. Strong cash generation underpinned both ongoing dividends and the special dividend declared in January 2026, while leaving the company with substantial cash and investments (see the next page).

Dividends declared for FY26 The total of ₹110 per share is made up of three interim dividends of ₹11 each (₹33), a special dividend of ₹46 and a proposed final dividend of ₹31. Market commentary noted that the final dividend of ₹31 was below the level some investors had expected. The proposed final dividend is subject to approval by shareholders at the Annual General Meeting. TCS has historically returned a large share of its free cash flow to shareholders through dividends and, in earlier years, share buybacks.
